transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-10-07 09:30 PT (recorded)
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nair (CTO, Oceanic Regulatory Labs), Lucas Reed (Head of IT), Marta Silva (Compliance), Tom Becker (Infra Manager)

Summary:
Quick intake to understand Oceanic's requirements for an air-gapped / on-prem Redwood Private deployment: hardware constraints, approval process for offline updates, network isolation, and compliance/audit expectations. Initial alignment on next steps and deliverables.

Topics covered:
- Air-gap packaging and offline update cadence
- Hardware compatibility (GPU SKUs, NICs, storage topology)
- HSM/KMS and key provisioning in offline environments
- Audit logs, retention, and SOC2/ISO expectations
- Canary/update rollback processes without inbound internet

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, and Diego our solutions engineer is here — we'll run through a few questions about your air-gapped needs.
[00:18] Priya Nair: Thanks, Maya. We appreciate it. Quick intro: Oceanic is a regulated lab doing marine biometrics research, lots of PII-ish metadata and internal patient-study artifacts, so we need a fully isolated environment. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private but leaning heavy to private / on-prem.
[00:36] Lucas Reed: Yeah, and from infra perspective we can't have outbound ports open from the inference nodes, approvals for an internet egress are months.
[00:44] Diego Alvarez: Totally understood, Lucas. We see that often. Couple quick clarifying q's before we dive deep — what's your expected peak throughput (rps or tokens/sec) and what's the model family you expect to run? Do you have a preferred GPU vendor?
[01:05] Tom Becker: Model-wise we'll be running a mix — large re-ranker and a T5-like for internal summarization, and some proprietary fine-tuned Llama-variant. We are currently standardizing on NVIDIA A40s and a few older V100s for cost reasons, but we're open to adding Ampere or newer if validated.
[01:28] Diego Alvarez: OK that helps. For A40s we typically recommend specific CUDA/driver combinations and a set of tuned kernels — in air-gapped setups we provide a packaged runtime that includes the validated drivers + runtime layers. We'll need to map exact driver versions to your NVMe layout.
[01:49] Priya Nair: One key question: how do offline updates work? We can't allow pull from the internet for model patches.
[01:57] Maya Chen: Great question. In our private/offline flow we ship signed artifacts — think tarball with a signature that your security team validates via a detached sig and our public cert. There's an operator tool that performs local install. For policy, updates can be staged on a jump box that has controlled transfer via USB or airlock procedure.
[02:21] Marta Silva: Sorry, can you repeat the signature flow? Our compliance team wants KMS-backed signatures.
[02:25] Diego Alvarez: Yeah, so the artifact is signed by Redwood's build infra. In more advanced deployments we integrate with the customer's HSM where we persist the verification key; you can do an on-site key ceremony and we can support verifying signatures against your HSM-managed keys. Note: in some transcripts the tool name appears as kay vee cache, but we mean KV cache — key/value.
[02:47] Lucas Reed: Couple of red flags: storage. We're mostly NVMe local with a 2-node storage head for redundancy, not a big SAN. How does Redwood handle model sharding and disk requirements?
[03:01] Diego Alvarez: Good note. We support model sharding across nodes and can stream weights from NVMe with mmap-friendly loaders. For low-latency, we recommend keeping the KV cache on local RAM or NVMe depending on model size. For multi-node setups we use a metastore to coordinate cache placements. We should run a capacity planning workshop to map model sizes to NVMe requirements.
[03:28] Tom Becker: Will the metastore need separate network connectivity?
[03:31] Diego Alvarez: It's typically over the private cluster network — no internet. We can operate over the cluster VLAN. But we'll want to confirm MTU sizes and NIC offload capabilities (RDMA optional) because that affects latency for multi-node.
[03:51] Priya Nair: On the compliance side, we need immutable audit logs for inference events, including token counts, input hashes, who requested, and which model version was served. Retention is 7 years for some data.
[04:07] Marta Silva: Right. And we need tamper-evident logs. Can you integrate with our Splunk/ELK?
[04:12] Maya Chen: Yes — our Private offering streams logs to local collectors (filebeat/td-agent). We can deliver cryptographic log chaining if needed and integrate with your SIEM. We'll share the log schema.
[04:24] Lucas Reed: Also curious about SSO and user management — SAML? OAuth?
[04:28] Diego Alvarez: We support SAML 2.0 for admin console SSO and can integrate Redwood Console access through your IdP. For service-level auth between internal services we use mTLS and token-based service accounts.
[04:40] Tom Becker: Any special network port requirements during install? We can't open many ports to the internet, but intra-cluster is fine.
[04:47] Maya Chen: For the installer itself, if you truly can't allow egress, the installer is fully offline. The typical install needs a jumpbox to transfer artifacts and container images. If you allow short-lived egress for initial validation, that reduces manual steps, but we can do full offline.
[05:03] Priya Nair: What about models — can we bring our own model artifacts? We have a fine-tuned Llama model with a custom tokenizer and proprietary vocab.
[05:12] Diego Alvarez: Yes, BYOM is supported. We will need the model format and tokenization routine. For quantized artifacts we recommend 4-bit or 8-bit profiles we have validated; your tokenizer/custom vocab will be bundled and verified. In air-gapped setups, we validate the artifact externally and provide a signed bundle that you import.
[05:32] Lucas Reed: Do you do any on-site support for installation?
[05:35] Maya Chen: For enterprise/private customers we offer a professional services engagement: on-site assistance, remote runbooks, and a handshake for the first deployment. That is usually contracted separately.
[05:47] Priya Nair: Another operational question: how are rollbacks handled if a model release causes regressions and we can't fetch a fallback from internet?
[05:55] Diego Alvarez: We strongly recommend keeping a local artifact repository with multiple pinned versions. Our rollout tooling in private mode can do canary/beacon deploys internally and automatically route to previous pinned versions if health checks fail. Since everything is local, rollback is just switching symlinks and restarting a small subset of nodes — but network and storage must be resilient.
[06:18] Marta Silva: On the audit front, who has access to logs? We need RBAC controls by role and also inclusion of approval workflows.
[06:25] Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports RBAC with granular roles plus SAML group sync. Approval workflows can be integrated via webhooks to your ticketing system, or you can have a manual signoff.
[06:38] Lucas Reed: For hardware, Diego mentioned drivers — can you supply validated driver bundles? Our policy prohibits arbitrary downloads onto nodes, so having vetted driver tarballs will help.
[06:50] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we provide validated driver + runtime bundles. In some prior installs we've provided signed OS packages and driver images that your infra team whitelists. We'll include checksums for validation.
[07:02] Tom Becker: Network isolation still worries me — what happens for downstream telemetry/metrics? We can't push telemetry externally, but need the observability data locally.
[07:11] Diego Alvarez: Our private deploy has a local metrics stack (Prometheus + Grafana) plus optional push gateways. You can choose to keep all telemetry onsite. For remote support, we can do a periodic masked snapshot that you export to us via secure transfer for debugging.
[07:28] Priya Nair: Any constraints on inference latency vs batching? Our workflows are sub-second for some queries, but others are batched overnight.
[07:37] Diego Alvarez: We recommend using dynamic batching with latency SLOs for interactive endpoints and heavy batching for offline jobs. In offline/on-prem environments you control the batching windows. For latency-critical flows, we tune kernel selection and avoid disk-based KV lookups. Also quantization choices affect CPU/GPU inference time.
[08:02] Maya Chen: Quick check — does your procurement need an initial budget number to route approvals?
[08:06] Priya Nair: Yes. A ballpark number that separates Dedicated-hosted pricing from Private on-prem capital + support is helpful.
[08:13] Maya Chen: We'll send a rough TCO showing monthly usage vs capex amortization for on-prem — Diego, can you surface the hardware SKU recommendations?
[08:20] Diego Alvarez: Yep, I'll include A40 and A100 options and an estimate for number of cards per expected QPS.
[08:26] Lucas Reed: One more: air-gapped vulnerability management — how do security patches get applied for the runtime?
[08:33] Diego Alvarez: We publish signed OS and runtime patch bundles on our release cadence. For critical CVEs, we can fast-track an emergency bundle. The bundle is applied via your change control process; we can do validation runs in a staging cluster first.
[08:49] Priya Nair: Can Redwood's runtime run on non-NVIDIA hardware? We have a couple of AMD MI250 boxes on prem intended for HPC workloads.
[08:58] Diego Alvarez: We have workstreams for AMD and other vendors but the validated path today is NVIDIA; AMD support is possible but requires additional validation and kernel work. We should capture that as a compatibility ask.
[09:12] Tom Becker: Any particular OS distros you recommend? We're predominantly on RHEL 8.5 and some Ubuntu 22.04 nodes.
[09:19] Diego Alvarez: RHEL and Ubuntu are both supported. For RHEL we supply RPMs; for Ubuntu we do debs. We'll list tested kernel versions in the compatibility matrix.
[09:28] Maya Chen: Let's talk about governance: who signs off on updates internally?
[09:31] Marta Silva: For compliance, updates to models or runtime require dual approvals: Security + Compliance signoff. We also require a rollback plan and regression tests.
[09:42] Maya Chen: Got it. We can include a recommended change-control runbook in the package.
[09:46] Lucas Reed: From a networking side, what ports are needed for cluster management vs model serving?
[09:50] Diego Alvarez: We'll provide a table. Typically HTTPS for console (configurable), mTLS ports for intra-service comms, and ephemeral ports for streaming. We'll try to minimize the surface area.
[10:02] Priya Nair: Anything about data residency? We will keep all model and input data on prem, but logs may need to be redacted before any export.
[10:10] Diego Alvarez: We support configurable redaction hooks and can apply deterministic hashing of PII fields before logs leave the cluster.
[10:18] Tom Becker: For the install timeline, what's realistic?
[10:21] Maya Chen: From contract to first deployment typically 8-12 weeks for new private installs including PS engagement, longer if custom kernel work is required.
[10:30] Priya Nair: Our internal legal wants to see indemnities for model behavior and data processing — is there an enterprise contract template?
[10:37] Maya Chen: Yes — our legal team has an enterprise template and we can share redlines.
[10:41] Marta Silva: Also need info on data deletion guarantees and revocation of keys.
[10:45] Diego Alvarez: We can provide a key revocation process. For complete model deletion we provide wipe scripts that remove cached weights and zero-out NVMe regions if required by policy.
[10:58] Lucas Reed: Perf question — can you run benchmarks on prem with our hardware?
[11:03] Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can. We'll package a lightweight benchmark harness that runs in your cluster and reports latency/throughput numbers. The harness can be run offline and the results exported.
[11:13] Tom Becker: Do you support multi-tenant on the same cluster? We might want separate namespaces for different research groups.
[11:19] Diego Alvarez: Yes, multi-tenant with resource quotas and RBAC per namespace is supported.
[11:25] Priya Nair: One last operational — retention and long-term archive of models: can Redwood integrate with our offline tape/archive strategy?
[11:31] Maya Chen: We can integrate with object storage connectors; for tape/archive we typically rely on your archival process importing the signed model bundles into tape. We'll document the archive workflow.
[11:41] (brief cross talk)
[11:50] Maya Chen: Alright, thinking about next steps — Diego will produce a hardware compatibility matrix; I'll share packaging spec and examples of our signed artifact flow. We'll also put together a TCO sketch.
[12:03] Priya Nair: That sounds good. Please include the compliance team on all docs.
[12:08] Marta Silva: Yes, cc me please.
[12:12] Maya Chen: Will do. Anything else from Oceanic?
[12:15] Lucas Reed: Not from infra, thanks.
[12:17] Tom Becker: No, that covers it.
[12:19] Diego Alvarez: We'll send the artifacts and schedule the capacity workshop — suggest week of Oct 20?
[12:24] Priya Nair: Week of Oct 20 works.
[12:27] Maya Chen: Great, we will follow up with calendar invites and share the docs. Thanks everyone.
